claim: DynamoDB transactions make coordinated, all-or-nothing changes to multiple items both within and across tables, and provide atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability (ACID).
question: What do DynamoDB transactions provide?

values.display: all-or-nothing changes to multiple items both within and across tables
atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID)

evidence.quote: Amazon DynamoDB transactions simplify the developer experience of making coordinated, all-or-nothing changes to multiple items both within and across tables. Transactions provide atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability (ACID) in DynamoDB, helping you to maintain data correctness in your applications.

claim: A TransactWriteItems operation groups Put, Update, Delete and ConditionCheck actions and either succeeds or fails as a unit; the same is true for a TransactGetItems operation of grouped Get actions.
question: How does TransactWriteItems treat the grouped actions?

values.display: either succeeds or fails as a unit

evidence.quote: You can then submit the actions as a single `TransactWriteItems` operation that either succeeds or fails as a unit. The same is true for multiple `Get` actions, which you can group and submit as a single `TransactGetItems` operation.

claim: There is no additional cost to enable transactions; you pay only for the reads or writes that are part of the transaction, and DynamoDB performs two underlying reads or writes of every item, one to prepare and one to commit.
question: What do DynamoDB transactions cost compared with standard reads and writes?

values.display: two underlying reads or writes of every item in the transaction
no additional cost to enable transactions

evidence.quote: There is no additional cost to enable transactions for your DynamoDB tables. You pay only for the reads or writes that are part of your transaction. DynamoDB performs two underlying reads or writes of every item in the transaction: one to prepare the transaction and one to commit the transaction.

claim: A transaction consumes its underlying read or write capacity even when the transaction does not succeed.
question: Is capacity consumed when a DynamoDB transaction fails?

values.display: consumed even when a transaction does not succeed

evidence.quote: This capacity is consumed even when a transaction does not succeed.

claim: The actions of a TransactWriteItems operation can target up to 100 distinct items in one or more DynamoDB tables within the same AWS account and in the same Region.
question: Can a single DynamoDB transaction span several Regions or accounts?

values.display: within the same AWS account and in the same Region
up to 100 distinct items

evidence.quote: These actions can target up to 100 distinct items in one or more DynamoDB tables within the same AWS account and in the same Region.

claim: Transactions cannot be performed using indexes.
question: Can a DynamoDB transaction target a secondary index?

values.display: Transactions cannot be performed using indexes

evidence.quote: Transactions cannot be performed using indexes.

claim: A TransactWriteItems operation differs from BatchWriteItem in that all the actions it contains must be completed successfully or no changes are made, whereas with BatchWriteItem only some of the actions might succeed.
question: How does TransactWriteItems differ from BatchWriteItem?

values.display: no changes are made at all
only some of the actions in the batch succeed

evidence.quote: A `TransactWriteItems` operation differs from a `BatchWriteItem` operation in that all the actions it contains must be completed successfully, or no changes are made at all. With a `BatchWriteItem` operation, it is possible that only some of the actions in the batch succeed while the others do not.

claim: You can optionally include a client token in a TransactWriteItems call to make sure that the request is idempotent, which helps prevent application errors if the same operation is submitted multiple times.
question: How do you make a TransactWriteItems request idempotent?

values.display: include a client token
helps prevent application errors if the same operation is submitted multiple times

evidence.quote: You can optionally include a client token when you make a `TransactWriteItems` call to make sure that the request is *idempotent*. Making your transactions idempotent helps prevent application errors if the same operation is submitted multiple times due to a connection time-out or other connectivity issue.

claim: Serializable isolation ensures that the results of multiple concurrent operations are the same as if no operation begins until the previous one has finished.
question: What does serializable isolation guarantee?

values.display: same as if no operation begins until the previous one has finished

evidence.quote: *Serializable* isolation ensures that the results of multiple concurrent operations are the same as if no operation begins until the previous one has finished.

claim: When a transaction completes, its changes start propagating gradually to global secondary indexes, streams and backups, so stream consumers should not assume transaction atomicity or ordering guarantees.
question: Can stream consumers rely on atomic ordering of the records of one transaction?

values.display: Stream consumers shouldn't assume transaction atomicity or ordering guarantees

evidence.quote: This propagation occurs gradually: stream records from the same transaction might appear at different times and could be interleaved with records from other transactions. Stream consumers shouldn't assume transaction atomicity or ordering guarantees.

claim: By default, the DynamoDB write operations PutItem and DeleteItem are unconditional: each operation overwrites an existing item that has the specified primary key.
question: Are DynamoDB writes conditional by default?

values.display: *unconditional*
overwrites an existing item that has the specified primary key

evidence.quote: By default, the DynamoDB write operations (`PutItem`, `DeleteItem`) are *unconditional*: Each operation overwrites an existing item that has the specified primary key.

claim: A conditional write succeeds only if the item attributes meet one or more expected conditions; otherwise it returns an error.
question: When does a conditional write succeed?

values.display: succeeds only if the item attributes meet one or more expected conditions

evidence.quote: A conditional write succeeds only if the item attributes meet one or more expected conditions. Otherwise, it returns an error.

claim: Conditional writes are helpful in cases where multiple users attempt to modify the same item, for example to make a PutItem succeed only if no item with the same primary key exists.
question: Why use a conditional write?

values.display: succeed only if there is not already an item with the same primary key

evidence.quote: Conditional writes are helpful in many situations. For example, you might want a `PutItem` operation to succeed only if there is not already an item with the same primary key.

claim: Optimistic locking is a strategy that detects conflicts at write time rather than preventing them, and each item includes a version attribute that increments with every update.
question: What is optimistic locking in DynamoDB?

values.display: detects conflicts at write time rather than preventing them
version attribute that increments with every update

evidence.quote: Optimistic locking is a strategy that detects conflicts at write time rather than preventing them. Each item includes a version attribute that increments with every update.

claim: With optimistic locking, if another process modified the item in the meantime, the condition fails and DynamoDB returns a ConditionalCheckFailedException.
question: What error does DynamoDB return when an optimistic locking version check fails?

values.display: `ConditionalCheckFailedException`
another process modified the item in the meantime

evidence.quote: If another process modified the item in the meantime, the condition fails and DynamoDB returns a `ConditionalCheckFailedException`.

claim: With an atomic counter, updates are not idempotent: the numeric value increments or decrements each time you call UpdateItem.
question: Is an UpdateItem atomic counter idempotent?

values.display: the updates are not idempotent
increments or decrements each time you call `UpdateItem`

evidence.quote: With an atomic counter, the updates are not idempotent. In other words, the numeric value increments or decrements each time you call `UpdateItem`.

claim: An atomic counter is not appropriate where overcounting or undercounting can't be tolerated, such as in a banking application; in that case it is safer to use a conditional update.
question: When should you use a conditional update instead of an atomic counter?

values.display: it is safer to use a conditional update instead of an atomic counter

evidence.quote: An atomic counter would not be appropriate where overcounting or undercounting can't be tolerated (for example, in a banking application). In this case, it is safer to use a conditional update instead of an atomic counter.

claim: BatchWriteItem does not support UpdateItem requests.
question: Can BatchWriteItem update an existing item?

values.display: `BatchWriteItem` does not support `UpdateItem` requests
